patient.name: Priya Chandrasekaran
patient.chiefComplaint: Severe headache and blurry vision, 36 weeks pregnant

history.hpi: Patient is 36 weeks pregnant (G2P1) and reports a severe, throbbing headache that started this morning and has not responded to acetaminophen, along with intermittent blurry vision and seeing spots over the last hour. Denies loss of consciousness or seizure activity. Reports mild right-upper-quadrant discomfort. No vaginal bleeding. Fetal movement felt normally per patient report.
pastMedical: Gestational hypertension diagnosed at 32 weeks, followed by OB
G1 prior pregnancy uncomplicated, term vaginal delivery
medications: Labetalol 100 mg PO BID (started 2 weeks ago for gestational hypertension)
history.lastOralIntake: Toast and tea approximately 3 hours prior to onset of headache
history.events: Husband called 911 after patient described worsening headache and new visual disturbance; he is present and appears anxious

scene.location: Second-floor apartment bedroom, patient seated upright on the edge of the bed
scene.safety: No hazards to crew noted; adequate room to work at bedside
scene.bystanders: Husband present, called 911 after patient reported worsening headache and new visual changes; provides history of gestational hypertension diagnosis
visualCues: Patient visibly uncomfortable, shielding eyes from light
Prenatal vitamin bottle and labetalol prescription bottle on nightstand
Patient periodically pauses mid-sentence, rubbing temples
No visible vaginal bleeding or fluid on bedding
Fundal height appears consistent with late third trimester

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 36-week pregnant female seated upright, alert and oriented, reporting a severe unremitting headache and new visual disturbances (spots, blurred vision). Initial blood pressure is markedly elevated.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, strong and regular
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities, no focal deficits
otherFindings: Severe frontal headache, 8/10, unrelieved by acetaminophen
Reports seeing spots and intermittent blurred vision over the last hour
No vaginal bleeding, no uterine rigidity, fundus soft and non-tender
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "My head is pounding and I keep seeing these spots — it's getting worse."

transitions.if: Severe features recognized, mag and labetalol given
transitions.condition: Crew recognizes SBP >160/DBP >110 with associated severe-feature symptoms (headache, visual changes, epigastric pain) as severe pre-eclampsia, initiates magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and treats the severe hypertension with labetalol after confirming HR is adequate.
Crew treats the severe hypertension with labetalol but does not initiate magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, leaving the patient unprotected against progression to eclampsia.

phases.name: Severe features recognized, mag and labetalol given
phases.description: Crew initiates continuous magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and administers labetalol to gently lower blood pressure toward a goal that preserves uterine perfusion, while positioning the patient left-lateral and reassessing frequently.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing severe hypertension (SBP >160/DBP >110) together with headache, visual changes, and epigastric tenderness as severe features of pre-eclampsia, the crew starts magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and gives labetalol to gradually reduce blood pressure.

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact, deep tendon reflexes 2+ and symmetric, no clonus
otherFindings: Positioned left-lateral to optimize uterine perfusion
Magnesium infusion running, IV fluids at 80 mL/hr per protocol maximum
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "The room doesn't feel as bright anymore, that's a little better."

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize severe pre-eclampsia: SBP 212/DBP 122 with headache, visual changes, epigastric pain
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Severe features of pre-eclampsia include: Severe hypertension (SBP greater than 160, DBP greater than 110); Headache; Vision changes including blurred vision, spots/floaters, loss of vision (these symptoms are often a precursor to seizure); Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain
expectedActions.rationale: Visual changes and headache with severe hypertension are precursor symptoms to eclamptic seizure and mandate immediate treatment.

expectedActions.shortAction: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20-30 min for seizure prophylaxis, then 2 g/hr infusion
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Magnesium sulfate: 4 g IV over 5–10 min, followed by 2 g/hr ... Seizure prophylaxis: 4 g IV over 20–30 minutes, followed by 2 g/hr IV if available
expectedActions.rationale: Magnesium significantly reduces the rate of progression from severe pre-eclampsia to eclamptic seizure.

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm HR >60, then labetalol 20 mg IV over 2 min; may repeat q10min x2
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Labetalol 20 mg IV over 2 minutes; May repeat every 10 minutes X 2 doses for persistent severe hypertension with preeclampsia symptoms; Goal is to reduce MAP by 20–25% initially; Ensure that HR is greater than 60 BPM prior to administration
expectedActions.rationale: Severely elevated blood pressure must be lowered to reduce maternal stroke risk while preserving uterine perfusion.

expectedActions.shortAction: Position patient left-lateral to optimize uterine perfusion
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients in second or third trimester of pregnancy should be transported on left side or with uterus manually displaced to left to ensure adequate uterine perfusion
expectedActions.rationale: Left-lateral positioning relieves aortocaval compression and improves placental blood flow.

expectedActions.shortAction: NS or LR IV fluids at maximum 80 mL/hr; high-flow oxygen as indicated
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: IV fluids: NS or LR – keep continuous infusion with maximum rate of fluids to 80 mL/hr. Administer high flow oxygen as indicated
expectedActions.rationale: Fluid restriction reduces risk of pulmonary edema, which is a recognized complication of severe pre-eclampsia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess blood pressure every 10 minutes during transport
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Reassess vital signs every 10 minutes during transport
expectedActions.rationale: Frequent reassessment guides repeat labetalol dosing and detects overcorrection or worsening hypertension.

transitions.if: BP trending toward goal, transport initiated
transitions.condition: Blood pressure trends down toward the goal of approximately 140/90 with ongoing magnesium infusion; patient transported emergently with receiving facility notified en route.

phases.name: BP trending toward goal, transport initiated
phases.description: Blood pressure is trending down toward goal with magnesium infusing and labetalol on board. Patient remains alert with improving headache, no seizure activity, and stable fetal movement reported. Emergent transport continues to the closest appropriate obstetric-capable facility.
phases.triggerCondition: After magnesium and labetalol are administered and vitals reassessed at the 10-minute mark, blood pressure is trending toward the 140/90 goal without overcorrection, and the patient remains seizure-free.

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact, deep tendon reflexes 2+ and symmetric, no clonus
otherFindings: Vision clearing, no new spots reported
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "The headache is still there but it's much less than before."

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport emergently to closest appropriate facility; notify en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport emergently to closest appropriate receiving facility – notify en route if possible so the receiving team can prepare
expectedActions.rationale: Advance notification allows the receiving OB team to prepare for a severe pre-eclampsia arrival capable of rapid decompensation.

phases.name: BP treated without magnesium prophylaxis
phases.description: The crew treats the severe hypertension with labetalol alone and does not initiate magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis. Without magnesium on board, the patient remains at high risk for eclamptic seizure despite blood pressure improvement.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew administers labetalol for the severe hypertension but omits magnesium sulfate; several minutes later the patient's visual disturbance worsens and she becomes unresponsive with tonic-clonic movements, consistent with eclamptic seizure.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Compromised by active tonic-clonic movement, teeth clenched
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Generalized tonic-clonic movements of all extremities
otherFindings: No magnesium on board at seizure onset
Active convulsive activity, unresponsive to verbal stimuli
Husband reports patient suddenly stiffened then began jerking

expectedActions.shortAction: Treat as eclampsia: magnesium sulfate 6 g IV over 5-10 min for active seizure management
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Any pregnant patient who is seizing should be assumed to have eclampsia and treated as such until arrival at the hospital ... Seizure Management: 6 g IV over 5–10 minutes or 8 g IM (4 grams in each buttock) to prevent seizure
expectedActions.rationale: Any seizure in a pregnant patient is treated as eclampsia; magnesium is first-line even after the seizure has already begun.
